newsitem.title: FRANCE: French forecast adds to European drought fears.
newsitem.headline: French forecast adds to European drought fears.

text.p: French weather forecasters added to mounting fears of drought in Western Europe with a warning on Thursday of another bone-dry week.

The meteorological service said rainfall had been as much as 50 percent below normal since January in the north of France and even lower in the south, where some regions had not seen a single drop of rain last month.
The news comes just days after French authorities called on farmers to turn down the taps two days a week in a clampdown on irrigation, and after similar predictions for Britain and Portugal.
Meteo France said it expected hardly a drop of rain for the next six days and that Marseille in the south of France had seen less rain than ever between the end of January and the eand of March.

Meteo France forecaster Franck Baraer told Reuters it was impossible to predict the pattern beyond a week and that rainfall levels were still slightly above those at this stage in 1976, which saw one of the most severe droughts in recent times. He said it would have to stay dry right through August for a repeat of the drought of 20 years ago.

Meteo France said in a statement that the south of France was now suffering from so-called agricultural drought, which starts to have a damaging impact on vegetation after about three weeks without rain but is reversible.
"The reason is the virtual absence of rain since January 25," it said.
Rivers and underground water resources in the south had so far been spared because of abundant rain last autumn and at the start of last winter, it said.
In the north, the lack of winter rainfalls for two years in a row was already taking its toll on underground water tables.
"Rainfall later on could push agricultural drought into retreat but the water tables will be unable to replenish before next autumn," it said.
Fears of prolonged drought in the grain regions of northern France pushed up the local price of wheat this week as traders worried about damage to crop yields.
The meteorological office said the lack of rain since the start of the year was mainly due to frequent anticyclones fending off Atlantic weather influences in both the north and south of the country.
Britain's meteorological office gave similar explanations and said the past 24 months had been the driest in the country since the mid-18th century.
